title: She Wanted a Promotion. She Did Not Want the Job.
author: Kelly
summary: A top-performing employee came asking for a promotion, but when her leader asked the right follow-up question, it became clear that she wanted the recognition and harder problems—not the travel, sprawling team, and life disruption the promotion would have forced on her. Kelly argues that a promotion is not a single reward but a bundle of a dozen distinct rewards welded together, and most employees reach for the whole package to access only one or two pieces they actually want. Leaders, in turn, hand the promotion over automatically because it is the only tool they think they have. The author 'unbundled' the promotion—giving the employee a genuinely hard problem and real money, without the life-disrupting elements—resulting in a happier, retained employee. A contrasting story illustrates what happens when leaders skip the follow-up question: an outstanding employee was promoted twice without being asked what he actually wanted, ultimately leading to burnout and near-resignation. The fix is simple but rare: ask not 'Do you want to move up?' but 'What are you reaching for, and what would you dread if it came attached?'—then build the reward accordingly.
points: A promotion bundles recognition, harder problems, money, scope, headcount, travel, and visibility into a single all-or-nothing package—most employees want only a few of those elements but must accept all of them to get the ones they value.

The 'unbundling' move—giving an employee the specific rewards they want (e.g., a hard problem with real money) while deliberately omitting what they don't want (travel, large team management)—is effective but rare because it falls outside standard org chart thinking.

The critical leadership question that prevents misaligned promotions is not 'Do you want to move up?' but 'What are you reaching for, and what would you dread if it came attached?'—a question most leaders never ask.
quotes: A promotion looks like one reward. It is actually a dozen, welded together and handed over as a unit.

It carries recognition. It carries challenges. It carries money and status. It also carries scope, and headcount, and travel, and visibility, and a whole new weight of expectation. Some of those a person wants badly. Others they would happily never take on.

People reach for the whole package to get the one or two rewards they actually came for. Recognition. A harder problem. Proof that they matter. A promotion is simply the only box the company gives them to check. They are not asking for the job. They are asking for the piece of it they want and bracing for the rest as the price.
Not “Do you want to move up?” but “What are you reaching for, and what would you dread if it came attached?

Growing your people does not always mean moving them up. Sometimes the most valuable thing you can do is ask what they are actually reaching for and then be the rare leader willing to give them exactly that and nothing they did not ask for.
